performers: Skidmore College Orchestra; cellist and conductor uncredited
intro: Elgar’s finale starts with a swagger, then the cello stops it in its tracks. Near the end, memories of the Adagio and the concerto’s opening break into the music before its last, abrupt rush.

sections.label: Intro · Orchestra, then cello recitative
sections.mNote: A brisk flourish leads to the soloist’s unhurried reply

sections.label: A · The cello takes up the march
sections.mNote: Allegro ma non troppo, marked risoluto

sections.label: B · Cello and orchestra trade phrases
sections.mNote: Short orchestral replies punctuate the cello’s longer lines

sections.label: C · Quick figures and singing cello
sections.mNote: The soloist moves between rapid runs and broad phrases

sections.label: D · The cello’s long lament
sections.mNote: The late solo grows through pauses and changing tempos

sections.label: E · The cello remembers
sections.mNote: The concerto’s opening recitative delays the final Allegro

sections.label: Coda · One last rush
sections.mNote: The Allegro returns to close in E minor

cues.title: The cello stops the march
cues.text: The orchestra starts briskly, but the cello soon takes its own time. Elgar writes Moderato, quasi recitativo: a speech-like solo, with pauses, chords and a sudden sweep across the strings. The finale has to wait while the soloist speaks.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, opening of movement IV and rehearsals 42–43: orchestral Allegro, then Moderato, quasi recitativo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/f/f6/IMSLP31083-PMLP14674-Elgar-Op085solo.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Risoluto: the cello joins in
cues.text: The cello takes up the finale’s brisk tune, marked risoluto — resolute. Accents give the phrase a swagger, and the orchestra answers it. Even here, Elgar keeps interrupting the march with little rests.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 9, rehearsals 44–46: Allegro ma non troppo, risoluto, accented solo phrases and orchestral replies.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A piano at Brinkwells
cues.text: In August 1918 Elgar has an old Steinway upright brought to Brinkwells, his Sussex cottage. He begins the Violin Sonata the next day, then writes the String Quartet and Piano Quintet. The Cello Concerto follows in 1919.
cues.evidence: Frank Beck, “Creating a Classic”, on the piano’s arrival and the sequence of chamber works and concerto: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Good and alive
cues.text: In July 1919 Elgar tells Sidney Colvin that he has nearly completed a cello concerto: “a real large work and I think good and alive”. He dedicates it to Sidney and Frances Colvin. On 8 August Alice posts the finished score from Fittleworth.
cues.evidence: Elgar to Sidney Colvin, late July 1919, quoted by Frank Beck; Alice’s posting of the score is dated 8 August in the same account: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm

cues.title: Too little rehearsal
cues.text: Felix Salmond gives the première at Queen’s Hall on 27 October 1919, with Elgar conducting. Albert Coates takes most of the available rehearsal for the rest of the programme. The concerto reaches its first audience underprepared.
cues.evidence: Première date and soloist: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-c.htm. Coates and the inadequate rehearsal: Adrian Jack’s BBC programme note, https://www.bbc.com/radio3/classical/elgar/notes/note_celloconc.shtml

cues.title: The cello takes its time
cues.text: Late in the finale, Elgar gives the cello room for an extended lament. The score asks it to broaden, press forward and linger again. Con passione appears over a phrase that pulls against the orchestra’s earlier march.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 14, rehearsals 66–71: Poco più lento, allargando, con passione and più tranquillo. Frank Beck describes the late solo meditation: https://www.elgar.org/3cello-a.htm
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: One last E-minor rush
cues.text: The finale’s tune rushes back, now marked Allegro molto. Cello and orchestra exchange short, forceful phrases and close the concerto in E minor. After the long solo meditation, the ending is startlingly brief.
cues.evidence: Novello solo-cello part, p. 14, rehearsals 73–74: Allegro molto and the E-minor close.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: He made the Enigma Variations from his friendships and preserved his own way with the music on gramophone records.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. His education continued in rehearsal rooms. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn from inside the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. Here was an orchestra whose players he knew individually, with capabilities he had to accommodate. His other work included teaching in local schools and giving private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
